title: PERMANENT RECORD
subtitle: The D1 registry and the write path

changes: Initial seven-module course on the location registry that TRANSMISSION PROTOCOLS reads from: why the registry left git for Cloudflare D1, the schema, the join that replaced a JSON column, the public write path and its validation, the collaborator gate, the materializer, and a capstone.

Assumes TRANSMISSION PROTOCOLS. HTTP, JSON, endpoints, the envelope and the KV serving copy are taught there and are not re-taught here; SQL and databases are assumed to be new and are taught from a plain baseline.
Audited against nc-zoning-board at 091b069, the same commit TRANSMISSION PROTOCOLS v2.2.0 pins.

contentAudit.auditNote: Course v1.0.0, authored 2026-08-02 against nczoning/nc-zoning-board at 091b069, read from origin/main rather than the local dev branch. Every project claim cites file+line at that commit: the nine migrations in worker/migrations, and worker/src/{validate,submissions,github-app,materialize,registry,audit,alerts}.js. The schema claims were read from the migration files, which are the authoritative statement of the schema, rather than from a dump of a live database, and the migrations carry their own reasoning in comments that this course quotes rather than paraphrases where the wording is load-bearing. Live shapes were ground-truthed with curl against api.nczoning.net on 2026-08-02: /v1/tags returns the 14 registry rows in sort_order, and /v1/locations returned 295 records of which 9 carry nexus- ids. Those two are the only D1 content this course can show a learner directly, because everything else it teaches is behind the collaborator gate. THE WRITE-PATH LABS ARE THEREFORE RECONSTRUCTED, NOT CAPTURED, and each says so in its own debrief; the shell runs every lab against canned responses with no live network, so nothing here can post a real submission. General concepts cite official docs (developers.cloudflare.com for D1 and Turnstile, sqlite.org for SQL semantics, MDN for status codes), verified 2026-08-02. The 'why' behind the design decisions comes from the NC-Zoning-Board project wiki, which is not a citable public source, so every such claim is carried back to the code or the migration comment that implements it. Two Board decision records are SUPERSEDED and were deliberately not taught from: cloudflare-worker-d1-submission-system (says git stays the source of truth; the git submission road was retired in 963f130) and api-version-semver-policy (describes the 1.3.0 backfill that was rolled back). Run `npm run freshness` to check the pinned commit.

chunks.heading: Field manual: what a database is, in one page
chunks.body: You already know the read side: a request, an envelope, a record. This course is about where those records come from, and it starts one level below anything the API showed you. A **database** is a program whose whole job is storing structured data and answering questions about it. This one is **D1**, Cloudflare's own, and it is **relational**: data lives in **tables**, a table is a set of **rows**, and every row in a table has the same named **columns**. A spreadsheet is a fair first picture: one sheet per table, one line per row, headed columns. You talk to it in **SQL** (Structured Query Language), a language of statements like `SELECT`, `INSERT` and `UPDATE`. The one idea that carries the rest of this course: a database does not just hold values, it **refuses** ones that break the rules you declared. That refusal, at the moment of writing, is the whole difference from a folder of files.

sources.label: Cloudflare - D1 (serverless SQL database)
Cloudflare - D1 SQL statements

chunks.heading: What it used to be
chunks.body: Until recently a location was a **file**. One JSON file per mod under `data/locations/`, edited by opening a pull request against the repository, checked by a script running in CI, and merged by a maintainer. A build step turned the folder into a single `mods.json`, the cron read that, and the map appeared. It worked, and it had one property worth naming: every change was a **commit**, so `git log` was a complete record of who changed what. Phase 6 of the migration deleted that folder, the build script and the merge path with it. The location registry is now `locations`, a table in D1, and the git history stops recording data changes from that day forward.

chunks.heading: Two stores, and only one of them is the truth
chunks.body: You met both of these in TRANSMISSION PROTOCOLS module 03, and the distinction is the spine of this course. **D1 is the registry of record.** A location exists there first, and if D1 is lost the data is lost with it. **KV is a derived serving copy.** The rebuild reads D1 and writes the result to KV; the read routes serve KV and never touch D1 at all. Delete the entire KV namespace and the next rebuild puts it back, which is why the config calls it recreatable at any time and calls D1 the opposite. The practical consequence for anything you write later: **fixing the map means fixing the row, not the copy.** Editing KV would work until the next rebuild overwrote it, roughly five minutes later, and the change would vanish with nothing to explain where it went.

sources.label: worker/wrangler.jsonc L73-82 (KV content is fully derived, recreate at any time)
worker/wrangler.jsonc L83-97 (the location registry, and the only source)

chunks.heading: Nothing auto-publishes any more
chunks.body: The old system had a second way in. A Nexus mod tagged `NCZoning`, carrying a formatted block in its description, was parsed and **became a pin** with nobody involved. That is over. A tagged mod is now a **candidate**: it appears in a list for a reviewer, it prefills a form, and it reaches the map only when a person approves it. The `NCZoning` tag is prefill, not publication. This is why the `source` field you saw removed from `/v1` in the other course could go: it recorded whether a record arrived manually or automatically, and once nothing arrives automatically the distinction stopped describing anything the system still produces.

quiz.prompt: A pin on the map is wrong. You have access to both stores. Where do you fix it?

options.text: The row in D1. The KV copy is rebuilt from it every five minutes.
options.feedback: Correct. D1 is the registry of record; the rebuild will carry the fix into KV on the next tick.

options.text: The KV entry, because that is what the API actually serves.
options.feedback: It is what the API serves, and that is exactly the trap. The next rebuild overwrites KV from D1, so the fix disappears within about five minutes and nothing reports why.

options.text: Both, so the fix takes effect immediately and survives.
options.feedback: Writing the derived copy buys you a few minutes and leaves a second place that can disagree with the truth. Fix the source and let the rebuild do its job.

options.text: Neither: open a pull request against data/locations/.

quiz.prompt: Which of these became the registry's responsibility BECAUSE the locations left git? Select all that apply.

scenario.title: FIELD REPORT // THE EDIT THAT UNDID ITSELF
situation: > [ TRAINING SCENARIO - constructed, grounded in the real rebuild cadence ]
> an operator fixes a misspelled location name directly in the KV entry
> the map shows the correction within seconds. ticket closed.
> 06 minutes later: the misspelling is back
> nothing failed. no alert fired. no log line mentions the name.

question.prompt: The correction reverted itself and nothing reported an error. What happened?

options.text: The 5-minute rebuild read D1, where the name was never changed, and overwrote the whole KV copy with the correct-by-definition version.
options.feedback: Correct. The rebuild does not merge, it replaces. Editing a derived store is always temporary, and it fails silently because from the rebuild's point of view nothing went wrong at all.

options.text: The KV write was rejected because KV is read-only.
options.feedback: It was not rejected: the map showed the correction, so the write landed. The problem is what happened to it afterwards.

options.text: Another operator reverted the change.
options.feedback: No person was involved, which is the point. This failure needs nobody to make a mistake beyond the first one.

scenario.debrief: The transferable rule: a derived store cannot be edited, only overwritten, and an edit to one fails in the quietest way a system can fail. There was no error because nothing erred. Ask of any store you are about to write to: is this the source, or a copy of the source? If it is a copy, find the source. Here that means the row in D1, and the rebuild carries it the rest of the way. (Constructed scenario. The cadence, the replace-not-merge rebuild and the two stores' roles are all real and cited below.)

sources.label: worker/wrangler.jsonc L98-109 (the 5-minute rebuild)
worker/src/materialize.js L1-17 (the only builder of the served dataset)

chunks.heading: The migrations are the schema
chunks.body: There is no separate document describing the database. There is a numbered list of **migrations**: SQL files applied in order, each one changing the schema, none of them edited once it has run. `0001_initial_schema.sql` creates everything; the eight after it change things. Read in order they are both the current shape and its history, which is why this course cites them rather than a dump of the live database: a dump tells you what is true, and the migration tells you why. One operational detail with teeth, stated in the first migration itself: named Wrangler environments inherit no bindings, so staging has its **own** database and every migration must be applied **twice**, once per database. Forget the second and staging drifts from production silently until something queries a column that is not there.

sources.label: worker/migrations/0001_initial_schema.sql L1-11 (applied to BOTH databases; every migration runs twice)
worker/wrangler.jsonc L88-97 (staging has its own database; named environments inherit nothing)

And `alerts` exists because a notification posted to a chat channel is not a record: it scrolls away, and the question 'has this been happening for a week?' has no answer unless something wrote it down.

chunks.heading: Four kinds of rule in that listing
chunks.body: Everything after a column's type is a **rule the database enforces on every write**, not a comment or a convention. `PRIMARY KEY` on `id` means no two rows may share one, so a duplicate insert is refused rather than stored. `NOT NULL` on `name`, `category`, `x` and `y` means a row without them cannot exist, which is why no code anywhere needs to handle a nameless location. `DEFAULT 'published'` fills a value in when the write does not supply one. And `CHECK (status IN ('published', 'hidden', 'draft'))` refuses any other string outright: `status: 'publishd'` is not a bug that ships, it is a write that fails. Below the table, `CREATE INDEX` declares no rule at all: an **index** is a lookup structure so the database can find matching rows without reading every one. These two exist because the rebuild filters on `status` and matches on `nexus_id` on every single cron tick, which is the only reason an index ever earns its cost.

sources.label: worker/migrations/0001_initial_schema.sql L15-44
worker/migrations/0001_initial_schema.sql L41-42 (why these two indexes: both run every cron tick)
SQLite - CREATE TABLE (PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, CHECK)

chunks.heading: status is not the same question as 'is it on the map'
chunks.body: `status` has three values and they are not a pipeline. `published` means the record is meant to be on the map. `hidden` means the pin is pulled but the record is kept, which is what you want when a mod is taken down and might come back. `draft` has never been published at all. The trap is reading `published` as 'therefore served'. It is not: the build can withhold a published record for a reason that has nothing to do with the row, and module 06 is about exactly that case. Keep the two questions apart from here on. **`status` is what an admin decided.** Whether a pin is served is what the build concluded, and the API reports any difference on `/v1/meta` rather than letting the two disagree quietly.

sources.label: worker/migrations/0001_initial_schema.sql L32-35 (the three statuses; hidden keeps the record)
worker/src/materialize.js L92-105 (only published rows reach the map, minus the withheld)

quiz.prompt: A write tries to store a location with status 'archived'. What happens?

options.text: The database refuses the write: the CHECK constraint permits only published, hidden and draft.

options.text: It is stored, and the build ignores any status it does not recognise.
options.feedback: It is never stored. A CHECK constraint is enforced by the database on write, not interpreted by the reader afterwards.

options.text: It is stored as NULL, because the value is invalid.

modules.title: ONE REPRESENTATION
modules.subtitle: How tags moved from a JSON column to a join, and how that was proven safe

lines: > subject: the same fact stored in two places

objectives: Explain what a join table is and what it makes impossible
Say why the old column was kept for five migrations after the join existed
Recognise a fallback that hides the failure it was written to survive

chunks.heading: A tag list as a string, and what it cannot do
chunks.body: At the start, a location's tags were a **JSON array stored in a column**: one text value reading `["house", "photos"]`. That is convenient and it has one fatal property. To the database it is just text. `"photos"` and `"photoss"` are equally valid strings, so a typo is stored happily and shows up as a tag that filters to nothing, months later, in a sidebar nobody is watching. The old system caught this with a script that ran in CI on data pull requests, which worked exactly as long as every edit was a pull request. Once edits became API calls, that check stopped standing between anyone and the registry.

chunks.heading: The join, and the rule inside it

sources.label: worker/migrations/0002_tags.sql L20-47 (tags, location_tags and the join index)
SQLite - foreign key support (REFERENCES, ON DELETE, ON UPDATE)

chunks.heading: What every line of that buys
chunks.body: A **join table** stores one row per link: this location carries this tag. `REFERENCES tags(slug)` makes it a **foreign key**, so the database refuses a link to a tag that does not exist. That is the point of the move: a typo'd tag stops being a thing that gets caught and becomes a thing that cannot be written. The composite `PRIMARY KEY (location_id, tag_slug)` means the same tag cannot be attached twice. `ON DELETE CASCADE` removes a location's links when the location goes, so no link outlives the thing it points at. `ON UPDATE CASCADE` handles the rare case where a slug genuinely has to change: one update propagates everywhere. And `slug` is the primary key rather than a numeric id on purpose, because the slug is already the identifier every record carries; adding an integer key would create a **second** identifier for the same thing, which is the exact duplication this whole migration exists to remove. The `name` column is what makes renaming safe: `neomilitarism` can display as `Neo-Militarism` without the identifier moving at all.

sources.label: worker/migrations/0002_tags.sql L16-19 (slug as the key, because an integer would be a SECOND identifier)
worker/migrations/0002_tags.sql L22-26 (name splits the label from the identifier)
worker/migrations/0002_tags.sql L37-39 (ON UPDATE CASCADE covers a slug that must genuinely change)

chunks.heading: Additive, then prove it, then drop
chunks.body: Migration 0002 created the join and **deliberately left `locations.tags` in place**. The old column stayed for five more migrations, until 0007 dropped it. That gap is the method, not hesitation. Dropping the column in 0002 would have made the join the new source of truth and simultaneously destroyed the only thing it could be checked against; the migration's own comment says it would be 'simultaneously the new source of truth and unverifiable'. Instead: add the new representation, switch the reader to it, run a **parity gate** that rebuilds the served dataset from the join and compares it byte for byte against the output the column produced, and only once that is green in both directions does the old one go. The rule generalises to any storage change: **you may have two representations, or you may have an unverified one, but the moment you have neither a comparison nor a rollback you have made the change unfalsifiable.**

sources.label: worker/migrations/0002_tags.sql L7-11 (ADDITIVE ONLY, and why dropping here would be unverifiable)
worker/migrations/0007_drop_locations_tags.sql L1-8 (dropped only once parity ran green, twice over)

chunks.heading: The fallback that had to die first
chunks.body: Migration 0007 could not simply drop the column, and the reasons are the most useful thing in this module. Two pieces of code were quietly depending on the old representation. The **importer**, which rebuilds a database from an export, listed `tags` in its insert and never wrote the join at all: dropping the column would have broken the restore path outright, and leaving it would have kept producing databases that serve every location untagged. And `resolveTags` **fell back** to the column when no join was supplied. That fallback sounds defensive and is the opposite: with the column gone it would have quietly served 297 records with no tags while looking like it worked. Both were fixed before the drop, the importer verified by building a database from nothing and counting 572 links against production's 572. The lesson is about the shape of the bug, not the tags: **a fallback converts a loud failure into a plausible wrong answer.** Where correctness matters more than uptime, throw instead.

scenario.title: INCIDENT LOG // THE RESTORE THAT SERVED NOTHING
situation: > rebuilding a database from the export, to test the restore path
> [import] 297 locations inserted. 0 errors.
> [import] done.
> [build] 297 records materialized. parity: FAIL
> every record served with tags: []

question.prompt: The import reported no errors and inserted every record. Why did every location come out untagged?

options.text: The importer wrote the old tags column and never wrote location_tags, and the materializer reads the join. Every insert succeeded; every link was missing.
options.feedback: Correct, and this is the real reason migration 0007 had to wait. The fix was verified by building a database from nothing and counting 572 links, exactly what production holds.

options.text: The tags table was empty, so the foreign keys refused every link.
options.feedback: That would have produced errors, not zero links inserted silently. The importer never attempted the links at all.

options.text: The parity gate is comparing against the wrong reference output.
options.feedback: The gate is doing its job: it found a real, total loss of tag data that the import step reported as a clean success.

scenario.debrief: Two rules come out of this one. First: **an operation that reports success has only told you it did what it was written to do**, which is a different claim from doing what you needed. The import genuinely inserted 297 rows. Second, and this is why the parity gate exists: the failure was invisible at every step except the byte-for-byte comparison. No error, no exception, a plausible-looking database, and 297 records serving an empty tag list. A count you can check against a known number, 572 links, is worth more than any number of green log lines. That is also why resolveTags now throws instead of falling back to an empty list: a missing join is a failure, and it should look like one.

modules.title: THE INTAKE
modules.subtitle: The public write route, and why validation lives on it

lines: > subject: the first public WRITE route on this API
> nothing here reaches the map. begin.

objectives: Trace a submission through its gates, in the order the Worker applies them
Explain why validation moved out of CI and onto the write path
Say what a 422 means here, and why a submission cannot set its own status

chunks.heading: Validation moved because the pull request did
chunks.body: Under the old system every write was a commit, so validation could be a **CI step**: a schema check run on the pull request, producing a red cross if a value was wrong. That arrangement quietly depended on one thing, and the migration removed it. A dashboard edit, an approved submission and an admin API call all reach the registry **without passing through a pull request**, so a check that only runs on pull requests now stands between almost nobody and the data. The gate therefore moved to where the writes actually are: the Worker validates every write **on the way in**, and a bad value is refused at submission with a **422** naming the fields, rather than accepted and caught later. Everything else in this module follows from that one relocation.

sources.label: worker/src/validate.js L1-14 (this IS the gate; nothing in CI sees a location before it is stored)
MDN - 422 Unprocessable Content

chunks.heading: The gates, in the order they run
rows: The IP hash salt must be set
503 submissions_unavailable
Without it nothing about the submitter may be stored; that is a server fault, not a bad request
Rate limit: 5 per address per hour
429 rate_limited
Before validation so a refusal cannot be used to probe the validator, and before Turnstile so a flood costs no verification calls
Turnstile token verified server-side
403, or 503 if verification is unavailable
The browser's token proves nothing until the server checks it
Field validation, shared with the admin editor
422 with the failing fields named
So a submission cannot express something the editor would refuse
Admin-only fields refused outright
status, admin_notes and source are writable by an admin, so a payload carrying them must be rejected, not ignored
chunks.body: The ordering is the interesting part, and each position is argued in the code rather than incidental. The rate limit sits ahead of everything expensive **and** ahead of everything informative: a flood is cheap to refuse, and an attacker cannot use refusals to learn what the validator accepts. Read the whole column of refusal codes together and it says something useful about the API's manners: `503` means we are broken, `429` means you are too fast, `403` means we do not believe you are a person, and `422` means we understood you perfectly and the contents are wrong.

chunks.heading: Refused, not ignored
chunks.body: Two rules in the validator are worth memorising because they are the same rule wearing different clothes. **Unknown fields are rejected, not discarded**: a payload with a misspelled field name is an error, because a typo that is silently thrown away looks exactly like a successful save. And **`id` cannot be set by a payload at all**. It is generated by the server on create and immutable afterwards, since letting a request choose it is how a deep link gets quietly repointed at a different mod. Both come from one principle: **when input is wrong, the system must say so rather than do its best.** Doing its best is how a submitter comes away believing they set something they did not.

chunks.heading: What a submission is, and what it is not
chunks.body: A successful `POST /submissions` produces exactly one thing: a row in the `submissions` table with status `pending`. It carries a `kind` of `create`, `edit` or `remove`, the proposed `payload`, an optional note and contact for the reviewer, and a **salted hash of the submitter's address**, never the address itself. That hash exists only for the rate limit and abuse triage, is purged after 90 days by the cron, and an unset salt fails the request closed, because an unsalted hash of an IPv4 address can be reversed by trying all four billion of them. What the row is **not** is a change. Nothing it says reaches the map until a collaborator approves it, and approval **re-validates the payload against the tag registry as it stands then**, not as it stood when the submission arrived: a tag can be renamed or removed while a submission sits in the queue.

modules.title: WHO IS ALLOWED
modules.subtitle: The collaborator gate, and a check with three answers

lines: > subject: authorisation. who may change the registry?
> [auth] collaborator check -> 204 yes / 404 no / 401 CANNOT SAY
> the third answer is the whole module. begin.

objectives: Say what the admin list actually is, and why it is not a list in the code
Explain why the Worker holds its own credential instead of using the user's
Name the three outcomes of the collaborator check and what folding them costs

chunks.heading: The admin list is the collaborator list
chunks.body: The registry needs an answer to 'is this signed-in person allowed to change the map?'. The answer chosen here is **repository collaborator status**: if GitHub says you are a collaborator on the project's repository, you are an admin. That is deliberate, and the alternative it beat is instructive. A hardcoded list of three logins needs no credential at all and is simpler in every way, except that it puts 'who is an admin' in a **deploy** rather than in a repo setting, and it starts silently disagreeing with the real collaborator list the moment either one changes. Making the collaborator list itself the source means adding an admin is a repo-collaborator change, with **no separate allowlist to drift**.

sources.label: worker/wrangler.jsonc L61-63 (the repo whose collaborator list IS the admin list)
GitHub REST - check if a user is a repository collaborator

chunks.heading: Why the Worker needs a credential of its own
chunks.body: The check runs **server-side, with the Worker's own credential**, and not with the token GitHub hands the user at sign-in. The reason is a permissions trap worth recognising in general: asking GitHub 'is this person a collaborator' with the *user's* token requires broad repository scope, which would mean an admin granting wide access to their repositories **merely to discover that they are an admin**. So the Worker holds its own identity. The choice there was between a **personal access token** and a **GitHub App**, and the App won on one property above all: a fine-grained token expires after at most a year, on a date nobody remembers, and when it dies the failure looks exactly like everyone having stopped being a collaborator at once. An App's installation token renews itself hourly and belongs to the organisation rather than to one person's account.

chunks.heading: Three outcomes, not two

sources.label: worker/src/github-app.js L134-156 (checkCollaborator returns yes, no or error)

chunks.heading: Never fold the third answer into the other two
chunks.body: 'Yes' and 'no' are the answers people design for. **'I could not find out' is a third answer**, and collapsing it into either of the others produces a specific disaster. Fold it into yes, by writing something like `not 404 means allow`, and a dead credential grants **everyone** administrative access, precisely at the moment the system is least able to notice. Fold it into no and a GitHub outage reads as every collaborator being quietly demoted, which is safe but silently wrong and sends people chasing a permissions bug that does not exist. So it is returned as **its own value**, and callers must do two things with it: **fail closed, and surface it.** Failing closed alone is not enough, because a security control that degrades into 'no' without saying so is indistinguishable from working.

chunks.heading: And then write down what they did
chunks.body: Authorisation answers who may act. The **audit log** answers who did. It is an append-only table, one row per change, recording the actor (a GitHub login, or `system` for the cron), the action, the target, and the record **before** and **after**. Never updated, never deleted: a correction is another row. Two details are worth carrying away. It exists specifically because the commit history stopped recording data changes when the registry left git, so this is not extra bookkeeping, it is a replacement for something that used to be free. And `before`/`after` are stored **verbatim, including admin-only notes**, which is right for the live table and wrong for any public export: the redaction belongs at the export, because storing a redacted copy would lose the actual history for the sake of a possible future publication.

quiz.prompt: Which implementation of the collaborator check is WRONG?

options.text: "return res.status !== 404" - anything that is not an explicit no counts as yes.
options.feedback: This is the wrong one, and it is the exact mistake the code warns about. A dead or unauthorised credential answers 401, which is not 404, so every caller would be granted admin at the moment the check stopped working.

options.text: Return 'yes' on 204, 'no' on 404, and 'error' on anything else.
options.feedback: Correct implementation: three outcomes, and the third is not disguised as either of the others.

options.text: On a 401, discard the cached installation token so the next attempt mints a fresh one.
options.feedback: Correct, and a useful detail: a 401 usually means the cached token has gone bad, so dropping it lets the system recover on the next request.

options.text: Run the check with the Worker's own App credential rather than the signed-in user's token.
options.feedback: Correct. Using the user's token would require broad repository scope just to answer whether they are an admin.

sources.label: worker/src/github-app.js L120-156

quiz.prompt: Why is the audit log append-only, with corrections written as new rows?

options.text: Because it is a history, and a history you can edit is only a claim about the past. It replaces the commit log the registry lost when it left git.
options.feedback: Correct. An editable record of who changed what is worth very little precisely when it matters most.

options.text: Because updating rows in D1 is expensive.
options.feedback: Cost is not the reason. The constraint is about what the table is for, not what it charges.

options.text: Because the table has no primary key to update by.
options.feedback: It has an integer primary key. Nothing prevents an update technically; it is a rule about what this table means.

sources.label: worker/src/audit.js L1-12

scenario.title: INCIDENT LOG // THE CREDENTIAL THAT DIED QUIETLY
situation: > [ TRAINING SCENARIO - constructed from the failure mode the code names ]
> a project gates admin access on a fine-grained personal access token
> the token reaches its expiry date. nobody had it in a calendar.
> [gate] github: HTTP 401 on every collaborator check
> the gate is written as: allow if the response is not 404

question.prompt: The token expired at midnight. What does the site look like at 00:01?

options.text: Every caller is an admin. 401 is not 404, so the check reads as yes for everyone, and nothing in the system notices that the question stopped being answered.
options.feedback: Correct, and it is the worst of the possible outcomes: the gate fails OPEN, silently, at the exact moment its credential died. This is why the real implementation returns a third value that callers must handle.

options.text: Nobody can sign in, so the dashboard is unreachable until the token is replaced.
options.feedback: That is what failing closed would look like, and it is the outcome you would want. This gate does the opposite because of how it reads the response.

options.text: The dashboard works normally: GitHub caches collaborator status.
options.feedback: There is no such cache standing in for the check. The 401 is the answer the gate acted on.

scenario.debrief: Two rules, and the second is the one people miss. **A check that cannot answer must not be read as an answer**: 'not an explicit no' is not the same as yes, and writing it that way turns a credential expiry into a full authorisation bypass. Second, **a credential with a fixed expiry is a scheduled outage you have not scheduled**, and its failure mode wears a disguise: everyone losing access at once looks like a permissions bug, not like a date passing. That is the specific reason a GitHub App was chosen over a personal token here. The App's installation token is short-lived by design and renews itself, so there is no date to remember and nothing to forget. (Constructed scenario. The 401 behaviour, the three-outcome return and the reasoning against a fixed-expiry token are all real and cited.)

sources.label: worker/src/github-app.js L120-133 (the 'not 404 -> allow' failure mode, named in the code)
worker/src/github-app.js L100-116 (the installation token is cached and re-minted a minute before expiry)

recap: The admin list is the repository's collaborator list, so adding an admin is a repo setting rather than a deploy.
The Worker holds a GitHub App credential of its own: the user's token would need broad scope, and a personal token expires on a date nobody remembers.
The check has three outcomes. 'Could not find out' must fail closed AND be surfaced, never folded into yes or no.

modules.title: THE MATERIALIZER
modules.subtitle: Turning rows into the served map, and withholding a pin without touching the row

lines: > subject: the last step. rows in, served records out.
> [build] locations.status: UNCHANGED. that is the point. begin.

objectives: Describe what the materializer does between D1 and the served dataset
Explain why a deleted mod's pin is withheld at build time rather than by writing status
Say why 'hidden' on Nexus cannot be automated and 'wastebinned' can

chunks.heading: The only builder
chunks.body: The **materializer** is the code that turns D1 rows into the record map the API serves, and it is the **only** thing that builds that dataset. It reads the published rows, joins each one's tags, works out its district from its coordinates, computes the recency flag against the clock, attaches the archive filenames, and hands the result to the refresh job to hash and store. One detail in it is stranger than it looks and worth knowing: the **order of the keys in each record is load-bearing**. JSON output follows insertion order, and the served payload is a public contract that was fixed byte for byte by the parity gate at the cutover, so a field written in a different position is a difference the gate will catch. That is why `archives` is appended after the record literal rather than sitting inside it.

sources.label: worker/src/materialize.js L1-17 (the only builder of the served dataset; the key order is load-bearing)
worker/src/materialize.js L131-166 (sort, district, recency, then the record literal)

chunks.heading: When a mod is deleted from Nexus
chunks.body: A pinned mod can disappear underneath the map. The cron asks Nexus about every pinned mod, and Nexus states a status. Three non-published outcomes are observable and they are **not** treated alike. `wastebinned` means deleted, which is unambiguous, so after **three consecutive sweeps** confirm it the pin is withheld from the built dataset. `hidden` gets a review-list entry and one alert, and nothing else. A mod simply **absent** from the response needs six sweeps and 24 hours before it is even mentioned, because absence is the only one of the three a Nexus failure can manufacture: a failed request returns no node, but it never returns a node saying `wastebinned`. Three sweeps is roughly fifteen minutes on a five-minute cron, and it is confirmation that the signal is real, not a grace period for anybody.

sources.label: worker/src/materialize.js L96-105 (records whose mod is confirmed deleted on consecutive sweeps)
worker/migrations/0009_nexus_mod_status.sql (the table that tracks consecutive sweeps)

chunks.heading: Withhold at build time, never by writing status
chunks.body: There were two ways to pull that pin. Write `locations.status = 'hidden'` from the cron, using the column that already exists. Or pass the withheld ids into the build and skip those records, **leaving the row completely untouched**. The second was chosen, and the reasons are worth more than the mechanism. **The invariant survives literally**: 'the only writers of `locations.status` are a human editing or approving' stays true, instead of becoming 'and also the cron, sometimes', which is the kind of exception that has to be remembered at every future reading of that column. **It self-heals**: if Nexus republishes the mod, the row is already correct, the withhold lifts and the next build serves the pin with nobody involved. Under the other design an admin has to notice and manually un-hide, and nothing tells them to. And **nothing needs undoing if the signal was wrong**, because the record is exactly as the admin left it.

sources.label: worker/src/materialize.js L96-101 (withheld HERE rather than by writing locations.status, so a reversal restores the pin with nobody involved)
worker/src/materialize.js L102-105 (published minus withheld, computed at build time)

chunks.heading: The cost: two true numbers that disagree
chunks.body: That design has a price and it was paid deliberately. **'Published in the registry' and 'served to the map' can now legitimately differ**, and the admin dashboard compares exactly those two numbers to warn about drift. Left alone, a withheld pin would make that alarm fire forever, and rebuilding would not clear it. So the drift row subtracts the withheld pins, and a rebuild the dashboard itself triggered reads as 'rebuilding after your change' in neutral rather than as drift in red. The reasoning behind that, from the code's own comment, is the transferable part: **a spurious alarm is worse than no alarm, because it trains the reader to dismiss it, and the one time it is real it looks identical.** This is also why the build **names** the withheld records on `/v1/meta` rather than counting them: 'three records withheld' is a number nobody can check.

sources.label: worker/src/materialize.js L168-176 (withheld reported by name, not counted)
worker/src/materialize.js L96-101 (a published record not served is otherwise a silent disagreement)

chunks.heading: And what a candidate is
chunks.body: The same pass produces the other list you have already met. Every mod tagged `NCZoning` that is **not** on the map and has **not** been dismissed is a **candidate**, published on `/v1/meta` as `skipped`. That definition changed: it used to mean only the mods whose metadata block failed to parse, back when a parseable block published a pin automatically. Nothing publishes from a block any more, so a mod carrying one is a candidate like any other, and filtering the list down to the broken ones would only hide work from the reviewer. If you took TRANSMISSION PROTOCOLS before this course, that is the change behind the `skipped` field you read there.

The second case is RECONSTRUCTED to show a candidate present. Note what /v1/meta does and does not tell a public reader: it publishes the candidates, and the withheld list is reported to the dashboard rather than to /v1, because a withheld pin is an operational fact about the build rather than part of the public record contract. The thing to carry forward is the reading habit. An empty skipped list is not the absence of information, it is a positive statement that nothing is waiting.

quiz.prompt: A mod is confirmed wastebinned on Nexus and its pin comes off the map. What happened to the row in locations?

options.text: Nothing. The build skipped it; status is still whatever the admin last set.
options.feedback: Correct, and that is what lets it self-heal. If Nexus republishes the mod, the withhold lifts and the pin returns with nobody involved.

options.text: status was set to 'hidden' by the cron.
options.feedback: That was the rejected design. It would make the cron a writer of a column whose only writers are meant to be human, and it would need an admin to notice and manually reverse it.

options.text: The row was deleted, and re-imported if the mod returns.
options.feedback: Deleting a record over a third party's action would destroy the coordinates, description and credits somebody wrote. Nothing here deletes on a signal.

quiz.prompt: Nexus reports a pinned mod as 'hidden' for three consecutive sweeps. What does the system do?

options.text: Adds it to a review list and raises one alert. The pin stays up, because a person has to read the author's reason.
options.feedback: Correct. 'hidden' covers an author mid-update and a serious moderation hold with the same string, and the API refuses to distinguish them, so no rule can infer the right response.

options.text: Withholds the pin, the same as wastebinned, because both mean the mod is unavailable.
options.feedback: Unavailable now is not the same as gone. Authors hide mods mid-update routinely, and the right answer is sometimes to repoint the pin at a successor mod rather than pull it.

options.text: Waits for a longer confirmation window and then withholds automatically.
options.feedback: Time does not resolve the ambiguity. A mod hidden for twenty minutes and one hidden for a month both need a person to read the reason; waiting only delays the cases that matter.

sources.label: worker/src/materialize.js L96-101 (only confirmed-deleted records are withheld)
worker/src/nexus.js L160-170 (an absent status field must read as published)

scenario.title: INCIDENT LOG // THE MOD THAT WAS NOT GONE
situation: > [sweep] nexus 28736 'Jig Jig Revolution': status hidden (sweep 3 of 3)
> [alert] pinned mod hidden. review required.
> author's stated reason, from the mod page:
> 'This mod is obsolete and should no longer be used. Please use this
>  mod instead: Jig Jig Unleashed - REVOLUTION.'

question.prompt: The mod is hidden and the author says it is obsolete. What is the correct action, and what does it say about automating this?

options.text: Repoint the pin at the successor mod. No rule could have inferred that from the status alone, which is exactly why 'hidden' waits for a person.
options.feedback: Correct. The map's real subject is the location, and the location still exists; only which mod delivers it has changed. Only someone reading the reason gets there.

options.text: Withhold the pin, since the mod should no longer be used.
options.feedback: That deletes a location from the map that is still perfectly available, just from a different mod. The player loses the place; nobody is protected.

options.text: Leave everything alone: the pin still points at a real mod page.
options.feedback: It points at a page telling players not to use it, which is a slow way to be wrong. The record needs updating, which is precisely the human action the alert asked for.

scenario.debrief: A real case, and the reason the deleted/hidden split exists at all. The generalisable rule: **automate on a signal that means one thing; escalate one that means several.** `wastebinned` means deleted and nothing else, so the system acts on it after confirming the signal is real. `hidden` is one string covering an author fixing an upload, a mod being superseded, and a moderation hold, and the API offers no field that distinguishes them. Building a rule on top of that ambiguity does not remove it, it just hides the judgement inside code where nobody can see it being made badly. Note also what the design bought here: because withholding never writes the row, none of this required an admin to remember to undo anything.

sources.label: worker/src/materialize.js L96-105 (only wastebinned withholds; everything else is a review entry)
worker/migrations/0009_nexus_mod_status.sql (per-mod status tracking across sweeps)

recap: The materializer is the only builder of the served dataset, and even its key order is fixed by the parity gate.
A confirmed-deleted mod's pin is withheld at build time and the row is never touched, so the pin returns on its own if the mod does.
Automate on an unambiguous signal, escalate an ambiguous one, and never let a system raise an alarm that is permanently true.

modules.title: REGISTRY CERTIFICATION
modules.subtitle: Capstone: a change arrives, and you decide what happens to it

lines: > NC-ACAD-02 // clearance check: LEVEL 7 // CERTIFICATION EXAM
> no new material. the registry is yours to reason about.
> you will be shown changes, refusals and disagreements.
> decide what is wrong, what is working, and what to touch.

objectives: Trace a change from a submission to a served pin, naming every gate on the way
Tell a real problem apart from the registry behaving exactly as designed
Choose the store, and the moment, at which a fix belongs

chunks.heading: The whole path, once
chunks.body: Everything this course covered lines up in one sequence. A person submits, and the Worker refuses them for cost, for humanity, and for correctness in that order. A pending row waits, carrying no authority. A collaborator is identified by GitHub, checked against the repository's collaborator list by the Worker's own credential, and either approved, refused, or told the check could not answer. On approval the payload is validated **again**, against the registry as it stands now, and becomes rows: a location, its tag links, and an audit entry naming who did it. Within five minutes the materializer reads those rows, decides which are served, and writes the result to KV, where the API you learned in the other course answers from. Nothing in that chain trusts the step before it, and every refusal on it says which step refused.

quiz.prompt: The admin dashboard says 296 records are published; the map serves 295. Nothing else is red. What is the most likely explanation?

options.feedback: Correct. 'Published in the registry' and 'served to the map' are different questions, and this is the case where they legitimately differ. The dashboard subtracts the withheld pins so the drift alarm does not fire permanently.

options.text: The rebuild failed and KV is a build behind.
options.feedback: That would show as discovery_stale, or as a heartbeat that stopped advancing. A clean build that serves one fewer record is a decision, not a failure.

quiz.prompt: Which of these statements about the registry is WRONG?

options.text: "A submission with a valid payload is applied to the map once the rate limit window clears."
options.feedback: This is the wrong one. Nothing a submission says reaches the map without a collaborator approving it. The rate limit governs how fast submissions arrive, never whether one takes effect.

options.text: "An unknown tag from an admin is refused; an unknown tag in a third-party Nexus description is dropped."
options.feedback: True, and deliberate. An admin typing a bad tag has made a mistake worth surfacing; a stranger's mod description has not.

options.text: "A correction to the audit log is written as another row."
options.feedback: True. It is append-only: never updated, never deleted.

options.text: "The KV dataset can be deleted entirely and rebuilt from D1."
options.feedback: True, and it is the definition of a derived store. The reverse is not true, which is why D1 has a nightly export and Time Travel behind it.

scenario.title: REGISTRY CERTIFICATION // MIXED SIGNAL
situation: > a contributor reports: 'I fixed a typo in a location name an hour ago. It is back.'
> audit_log: no entry for that location in the last 24 hours
> /v1/meta: discovery_stale false, skipped empty
> /v1/health: version 0.5.1, refresh_age_seconds 94
> the contributor is not a repository collaborator

question.prompt: Certification question: what happened, and what is the right action?

options.text: They never wrote to the registry. An empty audit log plus a healthy build means no change was applied, and as a non-collaborator they could only have submitted. Find their pending submission and review it.
options.feedback: Correct. Every signal here is green, and the audit log is the one that settles it: writes are recorded, so no entry means no write. Their edit is a pending submission waiting for someone with the gate's permission.

options.text: The rebuild overwrote their change: fix the row in D1 directly.
options.feedback: The rebuild does overwrite KV, but a change that reached D1 would have left an audit entry, and it would survive the rebuild. There is nothing in the registry to have been overwritten.

options.text: The build is serving a stale dataset: force a rebuild.
options.feedback: refresh_age_seconds is 94 on a five-minute cron and discovery_stale is false, so the build is healthy and current. Rebuilding would change nothing and would cost you the chance to read the signals properly.

options.text: Their submission was rejected by validation and the error was lost.
options.feedback: A refusal never creates a pending row and never reaches the registry, so this fits the audit log too. But it does not fit the report: they described making the change, not being refused, and a 422 is answered to their face while they are still on the form.

scenario.debrief: The reasoning to take away is the order you read the signals in. Start with the one that cannot be ambiguous: the audit log records every write, so an empty one for that record rules out every explanation involving a change that happened and then went away. Then the build's health rules out staleness. Then the person's role tells you which door they came through: a non-collaborator can submit, and submitting is not changing. This is the shape of most registry incidents. Not a failure, but a step somebody believed was further along than it was, and the system's own records saying so plainly to anyone who reads them in the right order.

sources.label: worker/src/audit.js L1-12 (every data change is recorded here, because git no longer records it)
worker/src/submissions.js L17-19 (a submission is not a change)

recap: Submit, gate, wait, authorise, re-validate, write the row and the audit entry, rebuild, serve. Nothing trusts the step before it.
Read the audit log first in any registry incident: writes are recorded, so no entry means no write.
The registry disagreeing with the map is sometimes the design working. Know which disagreements are designed before you fix one.
